Prologue.

The divine Augustine did not consider it a superfluous or vain thing to treat, in the sixth book of the City of God, of the fabulous theology of the gentiles. Because, as he says, once the fables and vain fictions that the gentiles held concerning their false gods were known, it would be easier to make them understand that those were not gods, nor could they give any benefit to the rational creature. For this purpose, in this third book, the fables and fictions that these natives held concerning their gods are set down, because once the vanities that they held concerning their lying gods are understood, they will come more easily, through Catholic doctrine, to know the true God; and so that they may know that those whom they held to be gods were not gods, but lying and deceiving devils. And if anyone thinks that these things are so forgotten and lost, and that the faith in one God is so founded and rooted among these natives that there will never be any need to speak of these matters, I believe that he thinks so piously; but let it be certain that the devil neither sleeps nor has forgotten the honor that these natives used to pay him, and that he is waiting for an opportunity, in case he might be able to return to the dominion he once held; and it will be an easy thing for him then to awaken the things that are said to be forgotten concerning idolatry. For this reason, it is good that we keep weapons ready, to go out to meet him. And for this purpose, not only will what is written in this third book be useful, but also what is written in the first, second, fourth, and fifth books. Nor will his followers have any opportunity to deceive the faithful and the preachers by gilding, with lies and pretenses, the vanities and baseness that they held concerning their gods and their worship; because the truths will appear pure and clear, declaring who their gods really were, and what services they commanded, as is contained in the books mentioned above.

End of the prologue.

Book 3.

¶Chapter one, on the origin
that the gods had.

Of the origin of the gods, there is no
clear or true account; nor
is anything at all known, but what is said
is: that there is a place called Te-
uticacan, and there, since time immemo-
rial, all the gods gathered,
and spoke together saying: Who is
to govern and rule the world?
Who is to be the sun? (and this has already been
discussed elsewhere). And at the time
when the sun was born and rose, all
the gods died, and none
remained of them: as will be told
further on, in the seventh book, in the
second chapter.

of Vitzilobuchtli.

¶Here begins the third book.

Chapter one, in which it is told
how the gods had their origin.

How the gods had their origin, where
they first arose, it is not well known, but
it is said that it was there at the place of
the gods' creation, they say that there,
in the time of darkness, all
the gods gathered together,
and they consulted among themselves
as to who should take charge, who
should bear the burden, who should become
the sun's lordship
(this is told separately for each). And when
the sun had appeared,
then all of them there died,
and were burned because of the sun: none
remained, none escaped death (as
it is told). And thus the elders
understood it. ¶Vitzilobuchtli was
greatly honored by the Mexica.
Thus they understood his origin
and his beginning: at Coatepec,
near Tula, in a single day it came to pass,
there lived a woman named Coatl-
icue: she was the mother of the Centzonuitznahua.
And their elder sister was named Coyolxauhqui.
And this Coatlicue there
did penance and swept,
she took care of
the sweeping.

Book 3.

...was called Coyolxauhqui: and the said Coatlicue did penance, sweeping every day on the hill of Coatepec. And one day it happened that, while she was sweeping, a little ball of feathers fell down to her, like a ball of spun thread, and she took it and placed it in her bosom, next to her belly, beneath her skirts; and after she had finished sweeping, she wanted to take it out and could not find it, from which, they say, she became pregnant. And when the said Centzonhuitznahua Indians saw that their mother was already pregnant, they became fiercely angry, saying: "Who got her pregnant? For she has disgraced us and shamed us." And the sister who was called Coyolxauhqui said to them: "Brothers, let us kill our mother, for she has disgraced us by becoming pregnant in secret." And after having learned of this, the said Coatlicue grieved greatly and grew fearful; and her child spoke to her and comforted her, saying: "Do not be afraid, for I know what I must do." And after hearing these words, the said Coatlicue's heart grew calm, and the heaviness she felt was lifted. And when the said Centzonhuitznahua Indians had made and finished their plan to kill their mother because of that disgrace and dishonor she had brought upon them, they were very angry, together with the sister called Coyolxauhqui, who urged them persistently to kill their mother Coatlicue. And the said...

(Nahuatl column, parallel account:)
Thus it was that she did penance on Coatepetl [Snake Mountain]. One day, as Coatlicue was sweeping, a ball of feathers came down upon her, like a tuft of down. At once Coatlicue picked it up and placed it in her bosom. When she had finished sweeping, she went to look for the feathers she had tucked into her bosom, but could no longer find them; thereupon she became pregnant. And when the Centzonhuitznahua saw that their mother was already pregnant, they grew very angry, saying: "Who did this to her? Who made her pregnant? She disgraces us, she shames us." And their sister Coyolxauhqui, very much given to anger, said to her brothers: "She disgraces us; let us kill our mother, the wicked one who is now pregnant—who did this to her?" And when Coatlicue learned of it, she was greatly frightened and deeply troubled. But the child within her womb spoke to her, calling to her, saying: "Do not be afraid; I already know what I must do." When Coatlicue heard her child's words, she was much comforted, her heart was set at ease, and thus she stopped worrying. And so, when the Centzonhuitznahua had agreed together and settled upon their plan, they resolved that they would kill their mother, and set about doing it...

Concerning the origin of the gods.                                   fo. 2.

The Centzonhuitznahua gods had taken up arms and were arming themselves to fight, twisting and binding their hair, like valiant men. And one of them, who was called Quahuitl Icac, who acted as a kind of traitor — whatever the said Centzonhuitznahua gods said, he would go and tell Huitzilopochtli, who was still in his mother's womb, giving him notice of it. And Huitzilopochtli would answer, saying: "O my uncle, watch what they do, and listen well to what they say, for I know what I must do." And after the council had finished its plan to kill the said Coatlicue, the said Centzonhuitznahua Indians went to where their mother Coatlicue was. And ahead of them went their sister Coyolxauhqui, and they went armed with all their weapons, banners, and bells, two by two, in their proper order. And the said Quahuitl Icac climbed the mountain to tell Huitzilopochtli that the said Centzonhuitznahua Indians were now coming to kill him. And Huitzilopochtli answered him, saying: "Watch carefully where they arrive." And the said Quahuitl Icac told him that they were now arriving at a place called Tzompantitlan. And Huitzilopochtli asked the said Quahuitl Icac further, saying: "Where have the Centzonhuitznahua Indians arrived?" And Quahuitl Icac told him that they were now arriving—

[Nahuatl text, continuing the same episode:] ...he became utterly enraged; his heart burned entirely with fury. Coyolxauhqui stirred them up greatly and provoked their anger, inciting the men to wrath so that they might die at once. Then the Centzonhuitznahua armed themselves for battle. And these Centzonhuitznahua, as their leaders, took up their war gear, bound their hair and their heads for war. And one of them, named Quahuitl Icac, went back and forth revealing their plans, telling whatever the Centzonhuitznahua discussed; then he would go and report it, counseling Huitzilopochtli. And Huitzilopochtli said to Quahuitl Icac, "Listen well, my uncle, to what I tell you; pay close attention to what I know." And when they had all agreed and united their resolve as one word — that they would seize her, that they would burn their mother — then their brave leader, Coyolxauhqui, armed herself completely, prepared herself for war; they equipped one another, distributing their war burdens among themselves, arraying themselves for the attack...

Book 3

...to another place called Coaxalpa. And once more Huitzilopochtli asked the aforementioned Quauitlicac, saying: "Where are they arriving?" And he answered him, saying: that they were now arriving at another place called Apetlac. And Huitzilopochtli asked the same Quauitlicac again, saying: "Where are they arriving?" and he answered him saying that they were now arriving at the middle of the mountain. And Huitzilopochtli spoke again, asking the same Quauitlicac: "Where are they arriving?" and he told him that they were now arriving, and that they were already very close; and ahead of them came the aforementioned Coyolxauhqui. And when the said Centzonhuitznahua Indians arrived, the said Huitzilopochtli was born at once, bringing with him a shield called teueuelli, with a dart and a staff of blue color; and his face was painted, and on his head he wore a tuft of feathers attached; and his left leg was thin and feathered, and both thighs were painted blue, and likewise his arms. And the said Huitzilopochtli told one of them, named Tochancalqui, to light a serpent made of torches, called Xiuhcoatl; and so he lit it, and with it the said Coyolxauhqui was wounded, from which she died, cut to pieces: and her head remained on that mountain called Coatepec, and her body fell down below, broken into pieces. And the said Huitzilopochtli rose up, armed himself, and went out against the said...

[Nahuatl column, parallel account:] She came girded with her net, her nettle-leaf garment, with painted paper hanging attached to her; and her bells were tied to her calves — these bells were called oyohualli — and her darts were gathered together. Then they came swiftly, in battle order, arrayed in ranks, going in formation, with Coyolxauhqui leading them, and Quauitlicac going ahead as a guide. Then he went running to warn Huitzilopochtli that they were coming. Then Huitzilopochtli said: "Watch carefully where they are coming." Then he told Quauitlicac: "They are now coming at Tzompantitlan." Again he reported to Huitzilopochtli that they were approaching. Then he said: "They are now coming at Coaxalpan." Again he reported to Huitzilopochtli: "Watch carefully where they are coming," and he told him: "They are now coming at Apetlac." Again he reported that they were coming, and he told Huitzilopochtli: "They are coming now, splitting through the mountain, approaching." And Huitzilopochtli again told Quauitlicac: "Watch carefully where they are coming."

...the Centzonhuitznahua, pursuing them and driving them out of that mountain called Coatepec, down to the bottom: fighting against them, and surrounding the said mountain four times. And the said Centzonhuitznahua Indians could not defend themselves nor prevail against the said Huitzilopochtli, nor do him any harm at all: and thus they were defeated, and many of them died.

And the said Centzonhuitznahua Indians begged and pleaded with the said Huitzilopochtli, telling him not to pursue them, and to withdraw from the battle. But the said Huitzilopochtli would not, nor did he consent, until he had killed almost all of them, and very few escaped; and they fled from his hands, and went to a place called Huitztlampa: and he took from them and seized many spoils, and the weapons they carried, which were called Anecuyotl. The said Huitzilopochtli was also called Tetzahuitl, for the reason that they say the serpent Coatlicue became pregnant from a little ball of feathers, and it was not known who his father was. And the said Mexicans have held him in great reverence, and have served him in many ways, and have regarded him as the god of war, because they said that the said Huitzilopochtli gave them great favor in battle; and the order and custom that the Mexicans kept, in order to serve and honor him...

Then immediately he struck down at Cuauhtlicac; then he fell swiftly upon the town, then he reached and arrived, raging, at Coyolxauhqui. And Huitzilopochtli then entered; then he took up his equipment, his shield, his tehuehuelli, and his darts, and his atlatl, the blue one, called the fire-serpent (xiuhcoatl); and with it he thrust into her legs, thus her thighs were cut apart — it is told how he worked his vengeance. It is said that this was his boy's ornament; he was adorned with down upon his head, upon his forehead, and upon his ears. And one of his darts was slender on the left side, feathered, upon the sole of his foot; and both his thighs were painted blue, and both his shoulders as well. And one named Tochancalqui set fire with the fire-serpent, by the command of Huitzilopochtli; then he struck Coyolxauhqui; and then quickly they cut off her head. Her head remained there on the slope of Coatepetl. And her body, falling down below, shattered to pieces as it fell; here and there fell her hand, her foot, and her body. And Huitzilopochtli then rose up in triumph and gave chase...

The said Huitzilopochtli took up that which was customarily used and done on that aforementioned mountain range, which is named Coatepec.

...when it came down, they made it descend, the people of the town came out, the Centzonhuitznahua, atop Coatepec. And when they threw it down to the ground, to the base, then they pursued it, they circled around it, they circled around Coatepec; four times they went around it in pursuit, they circled around it in pursuit, in vain did they try to encircle it, in vain did they wish to surround it, they struck their shields, but it was of no use, nothing could they do, nothing could they achieve, they could no longer hold it back, for Huitzilopochtli had already shown himself: he scattered them upon the mountain, he destroyed them, he blinded them, he smoked them out entirely. And thus they could no longer leave them in peace, in everything they clung to them, greatly did they beg him, they said to him, "let it be enough." But Huitzilopochtli was not moved to pity, with great force he pursued them. And wherever they turned to flee from him, wherever each one of them went to stand facing him, for that reason they stood facing him, the Centzonhuitznahua, wherever they each went, into his hands they fell before Huitzilopochtli. And as soon as he had killed them, as soon as he had finished with them, he took away their belongings from them, their adornments, their equipment, he made them his own property, he made them his possessions, he made them his insignia, thus he put them on as his finery. And Huitzilopochtli was called "the dreadful one," because he was indeed terrible...

¶ Second paragraph, on how they honored Huitzilopochtli as a farewell.

Likewise they say that on the day when they kneaded and shaped the body of Huitzilopochtli, in order to celebrate the feast called Panquetzaliztli, they took amaranth seeds and cleaned them very carefully, removing the straw and setting aside other seeds, which are called petzicatl and tezcaoauhtli; and they ground these very finely. And after they had been ground, when the flour was very fine, they kneaded it to make the body of the said Huitzilopochtli. And the next day, a man called Quetzalcoatl shot an arrow into the body of the said Huitzilopochtli — a dart tipped with a stone point — and it was thrust into his heart, while the king or lord was present; and a kinsman of the said Huitzilopochtli, who was called Teuoa, was also present, along with four great [men]...

[Nahuatl column, continuing from the previous page and beginning a new section:]

...there in the lower region, at its base, where its mother dwelt, at Coatepetl. He it was who was kept and venerated by the Mexica as their god; they worshipped him, served him, and all things pertaining to him were done in his honor as Huitzilopochtli. And such was the great reverence that was given him there at Coatepetl, as it was done from ancient times until the present, in its entirety.

¶ Here begins the third paragraph, concerning how they venerated Huitzilopochtli, how they worshipped him as a god.

And as for Huitzilopochtli — when the day arrived on which his body, his likeness, was to be made, in the month called Panquetzaliztli, they made the amaranth-seed dough image. They formed it with great care, grinding the seeds very finely, kneading and shaping it, forming and refashioning it, molding it like a man, like an arrow; they removed the amaranth seeds, reworking it very skillfully, making it entirely of fine amaranth dough, together with the toasted maize, the seed grains, and the small amaranth-dough figures, which they also carefully made and formed with great skill. And the dough image was made the way bread is made, mixed with maguey wine, shaped as a human figure. And the next day the body of Huitzilopochtli was 'slain' — that is, the dough image was ritually sacrificed...

Book 3

...priests: and besides, four other principal men, of the youths, who had charge of raising the young men: these were called telpochtlatoque. All these were present when they killed the body [effigy] of Huitzilopochtli. And after the said Huitzilopochtli had been "killed," they then took apart and dismantled the body of Huitzilopochtli, which was a dough made of amaranth seed; and the heart of Huitzilopochtli they took for the lord, or king; and all the rest of the body, and the pieces, which were like bones, of the said Huitzilopochtli, were divided into two parts among the natives of Mexico and of Tlatelolco. Those of Mexico, who were ministers of the said Huitzilopochtli and who were called calpules, took four pieces of the body of the said Huitzilopochtli, and the same amount was taken by those of Tlatelolco, who were likewise called calpules. And thus, in this manner, they divided among themselves the four pieces of the body of Huitzilopochtli: to the people of the two wards, and to the ministers of the idols, who were called calpules; these ate the body of Huitzilopochtli each year, according to their order and custom which they had kept. Each one ate a small piece of the body of Huitzilopochtli; and those who ate it were young men, and they said that it was the body of god, which was called teocualo ["the eating of the god"]; and those who received and ate the body of Huitzilopochtli were called ministers of god.

[Nahuatl text, parallel in content:] ...it was [the feast] of Quetzalcoatl: and when they killed it with an arrow, piercing it at the top of the head, they placed it [the arrow] into its heart, before the dying image of Motecuzoma, and his attendants, who were those who had charge of Huitzilopochtli, who prepared it, who arranged it in order, and the eldest brothers, the leaders, so that all of them died there before the presence of Huitzilopochtli. And when it was dead, they then broke apart its dough body, and its heart was reserved for Motecuzoma; and the rest of the pieces, like bones, became [the sacred remains], were divided and given out among the people, divided between the hands of the Tlatelolca, and also for the makers of the litter/platform; likewise it was given into the hands of the elders of the calpulli of the Tlatelolca, and the same was given into the hands of the Tenochca. And afterward, they distributed it among themselves, as a duty owed for the year. Each year they ate it; one year they ate it in the ward-house (tlaxilacalli), another year in the calpulli of the elders of the calpulli. And what they gave to eat was of the flesh of the amaranth-dough image, very small pieces, tiny bits, small morsels. These were eaten by the young men. And this eating was called teocualo ["the eating of the god"]. And because they ate it, it was called the sacred/divine matter.

Third paragraph, concerning the penance to which those who received the body of Huitzilopochtli were obligated.

The young men who received and ate the body of the said Huitzilopochtli were obligated to serve for one year: and every night they lit fires, and spent a great quantity of firewood, which amounted to more than two thousand sticks and more; which cost them ten large blankets, called quachtli, from which they suffered great hardship and trouble. Each one was obligated to pay one large blanket, called quachtli, and five small blankets, called tequachtli, as well as a basket of maize and a hundred ears of maize. Those who could not pay, feeling themselves greatly burdened by this tribute, would flee; and some resolved to die in war, at the hands of the enemy. And when the said young men knew that they were finishing and fulfilling the service and penance to which they were obligated, among themselves they once again collected another tribute: each one paid six small blankets, called tequachtli, with which they bought torches, firewood, and everything necessary to honor the said Huitzilopochtli at the end of the year. Third paragraph, in which is told the penance that was performed, that was carried out, in order to eat the flesh of Huitzilopochtli.

And for an entire year this great self-affliction was performed. And for a full year they kept the fast of the incense offerings; there every night much wood was burned — bundles amounting to five hundred, eight hundred of pine torches, the next day and the next, together with ten blankets. With this they suffered, they were made to endure hardship; and each one was required to provide one blanket and five small blankets, then also a basket of shelled maize, and a hundred ears of maize each person had to furnish. With this they clothed themselves, they suffered affliction, they were made poor. And some of them fled, thereby becoming fugitives, going off somewhere. And those who died, who threw themselves into war, died in war there, hurling themselves against their enemies. And when the time came for them to end this death-penance, it was their duty to render a final accounting, each one...

Book 3

On the day when they washed the said Vitzilobuchtli, it was midnight; and before they washed him, first they held a procession called necocololo. One man dressed himself in the garments of the said Vitzilobuchtli; he was called yiopuch, and he went dancing in the person of Vitzilobuchtli. Before him went one who was called vitznaoac tiachcauh, and behind him went all the principal men among the youths, who are called tiachcauhtlatoque, and brave men; and other people all together behind, with pine-torch candles, as far as the place where the said Vitzilobuchtli was to be washed, which was called ayauhcalo, and they played flutes for him.

Then they seated the said Vitzilobuchtli, and the priest in charge of the said Vitzilobuchtli, who was called teuoa, took the water in a painted gourd cup, of a blue color, four times, and set it before him with four green reeds, and washed the face of the said Vitzilobuchtli, and his whole body.

And after the washing, the one who was dressed in the garments of the said Vitzilobuchtli took up the statue of the said Vitzilobuchtli again, [carrying] the flutes, and carried it until he placed and seated it in the temple. And thus, after having placed the statue of the said Vitzilobuchtli, they all then went out and went to their houses. And from this...

[The Nahuatl text, running parallel, recounts the same ceremony in Classical Nahuatl: describing the yearly ritual preparations, the making of offerings of wood and stone altars, the bathing of the image of Vitzilobuchtli at midnight marking the completion of a year, the adornment of a man as the likeness (ixiptla) of the god called Ysobuch, the dancing and processions of the young warriors and leaders (tiachcauhti, telpochtequioa), the carrying of torches and playing of flutes, and the ritual bathing and placing of the image of Vitzilobuchtli in its place, followed by further rites performed by the priests (teuhoa).]

Fourth paragraph, concerning another very heavy tribute: which was paid by those who ate the body of Huitzilopochtli.

When the said year had ended, other young men then began to oblige themselves to serve and to do penance: according to the order and custom that governed how they were to eat and receive the body of the said Huitzilopochtli. And together with the ministers of the idols, who are called calpules: they performed great service and penance, from which they suffered the greatest hardship,

[Nahuatl column, paralleling the above, describing in ritual detail how water was taken and poured in a green vessel, offered with feathers before (the image), then the flesh, green and raw, was placed four times into the vessel together with the water, and with it they bathed; and having bathed, again they took up the (reed/sign?) which they carried, striking it loudly; and then they carried it to where they placed it before the idol; and having set it down, then the fasting and the singing took place, with which their abstinence and penance, the eating of the teuquaque, ended for that year.

Here begins the fourth paragraph, where is told another very heavy duty, which was performed by those who received the flesh of Huitzilopochtli.

Likewise another group then began this: in that year, those destined to be teuquaque would separate themselves, and they would go on in this way, year by year, taking turns, distributing themselves among each other, going about with feathers, going about scattering themselves in different places; and likewise, the leaders of the calpulli, each year, would...]

Book 3

...and fatigue, which could not be endured, because every night throughout the entire year they spent and consumed a great and excessive quantity of firewood and torches, of the finest kind, and chili peppers, and tomatoes, and salt, and squash seeds, and cacao almonds, and food. And when these ran short, so that they could buy the necessary things, they sold the cloaks they wore, or bought on credit, or asked to borrow something: or they sold the irrigated lands, or the lands of the hills, which had been assigned to the idols, whom they served. And whoever could not pay the tribute immediately left the lands behind. And when the time came that they knew they had fulfilled and completed the penance and service to which they were obligated, in serving the said Huitzilopochtli, they washed and cleaned themselves, and made festive food: tamales and some well-cooked stews; or they killed a small dog which they ate, and they got drunk, for the reason that they had completed the service and penance to which they were obligated — because the tribute seemed to them very heavy indeed, like a burden that could barely be carried. And thus afterward they rejoiced greatly, because now they were free from the great labor and hardship; and they slept peacefully and tranquilly, and freely sought their livelihood: and they worked at fishing, or processed the maguey...

[The parallel Nahuatl text, continuing the same account in the native language, describes how the people greatly afflicted and impoverished themselves, suffered hunger and want, burned themselves with torches, consumed much wood and resin for light, prepared chili, tomatoes, salt, chia seed, and water as food; how they wrapped themselves in their cloaks, sold or pawned their land, or settled debts among kin; how some gave up their land, their chinampas, their irrigated or humid fields, or their maize fields because of the burden of tribute; and how when the period of fasting concluded, there was great rejoicing...]

...of eating and drinking and riches. And the said Titlacauan was invisible, and like darkness and air; and when he appeared or spoke to some man, he was like a shadow, and he knew the secrets that men held in their hearts; and they acclaimed him, praying and saying to him: "O powerful god, who gives life to men, you who are called Titlacauan, have mercy on me and grant me everything necessary to eat and drink, and to enjoy your sweetness and delight, because I suffer great hardship and need in this world. Have mercy on me, for I am so poor and naked, and I labor to serve you; for your service I sweep, and clean, and light fires in this poor house where I wait for whatever you may command me. Or else let me die soon, and let this toilsome and miserable life end, so that my body may rest and find repose."
